summary: Eugene Yan, Principal Applied Scientist at Amazon, delivers a keynote on merging recommendation systems with language models. He traces language modeling in RecSys from Word2vec (2013) through GRUs for short-term sequence prediction and Transformers for long-range dependencies. He identifies three challenges and solutions. First, hash-based item IDs fail to encode content, causing cold start and sparsity. Semantic IDs solve this, demonstrated by Kuaishou's multimodal approach concatenating ResNet, BERT, and VGGish embeddings, clustered via k-means into 1,000 cluster IDs from 100M videos, increasing cold-start coverage by 3.6%. Second, data quality at scale is costly. LLMs excel at synthetic data generation. Indeed's iterative journey from open models to GPT-4 to a distilled lightweight classifier achieved 0.86 AUROC, cutting bad recommendations 20%, increasing application rate 4%, and reducing unsubscribe rate 5%. Spotify used LLMs to generate natural language exploratory queries for new content categories (podcasts, audiobooks), combining them with conventional query mining from search logs and catalog titles. This achieved +9% exploratory queries, enabling one-tenth of users to explore new products daily. Third, separate systems for ads, recommendations, and search create duplicative pipelines and maintenance costs. Unified models address this. Netflix's Unicorn unified contextual ranker takes unified input (user ID, item ID, search query, country, task) and uses smart imputation (e.g., using item title as search query for item-to-item recommendations). It matched or exceeded specialized models across multiple tasks, removing tech debt. Etsy's unified embeddings use T5 text embeddings, shared token encoders for product category and user location, and a quality vector concatenated to product embeddings for ratings, freshness, and conversion rate. This achieved 2.6% site-wide conversion increase and 5%+ search purchase increase. Yan notes alignment tax may require splitting into multiple unified models.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction: Language Modeling in RecSys
sections.summary: Yan introduces the talk with dog-themed slides (Latte and Mochi). He traces language modeling in RecSys from Word2vec (2013) for item embeddings, through GRUs for short-term sequence prediction, to Transformers for long-range dependencies across long user sequences. He previews three key ideas: semantic IDs, data augmentation, and unified models.

sections.title: Challenge 1 & Solution: Hash-based IDs and Semantic IDs (Kuaishou)
sections.summary: Hash-based item IDs don't encode content, causing cold start and sparsity. Kuaishou's solution: a two-tower network with multimodal content inputs (ResNet for visual, BERT for text, VGGish for audio), concatenated and clustered via k-means into 1,000 cluster IDs from 100M videos. Trainable cluster IDs mapped to embedding tables learn to map content space to behavioral space. Results: outperformed hash-based IDs on clicks/likes, increased cold-start coverage by 3.6%, and improved cold-start velocity.

sections.title: Challenge 2 & Solution: Data Augmentation and LLM-Augmented Synthetic Data
sections.summary: Data quality at scale is the lifeblood of ML, especially for search (metadata, query expansion, synonyms, spellchecking). Traditional methods like human annotation are costly. LLMs excel at generating synthetic data and labels. Two case studies previewed: Indeed and Spotify.

sections.title: Indeed Case Study: Filtering Bad Job Recommendations
sections.summary: Indeed faced bad email job recommendations causing user distrust and unsubscriptions. Their iterative solution: expert labels, then open models (Mistral, Llama 2) which performed poorly, then GPT-4 (90% precision/recall but 32s latency), then GPT-3.5 (63% precision), then fine-tuned GPT-3.5 (0.93 precision, 6.7s, still too slow), finally distilling a lightweight classifier (0.86 AUROC, sub-200ms). Outcome: 20% fewer bad recs, 4% higher application rate, 5% lower unsubscribe rate, proving quality over quantity.

sections.title: Spotify Case Study: Query Recommendation for New Content Categories
sections.summary: Spotify introduced podcasts and audiobooks beyond music, creating cold-start on new categories. Their query recommendation system combines conventional query mining from search logs and catalog titles with LLM-generated natural language queries. Yan emphasizes using LLMs to augment proven techniques rather than replacing everything. Exploratory queries are ranked alongside immediate results, informing users of new categories without banners. Result: +9% exploratory queries, with one-tenth of users exploring new products daily, enabling rapid category growth.

sections.title: Challenge 3 & Solution: Separate Systems and Unified Models
sections.summary: Companies typically maintain separate systems for ads, recommendations, and search, and even multiple recommendation models for different surfaces (homepage, item-to-item, thank-you page). This creates duplicative engineering pipelines, high maintenance costs, and no transfer of improvements between models. The solution is unified models, analogous to foundation models in vision and language. Yan cites Stripe's transformer-based payments fraud model as an example beyond RecSys.

sections.title: Netflix Case Study: Unicorn Unified Contextual Ranker
sections.summary: Netflix built Unicorn, a unified contextual ranker, to replace bespoke models for search, similar-item recommendations, and pre-query recommendations. It uses a user foundation model fed by watch history plus a context and relevance model. Unified input includes user ID, item ID, search query, country, and task. Smart imputation handles missing inputs (e.g., using current item title as search query for item-to-item recommendations). The unified model matched or exceeded specialized models on multiple tasks, removing tech debt and enabling faster iteration.

sections.title: Etsy Case Study: Unified Embeddings for Search
sections.summary: Etsy faced challenges with specific queries (e.g., 'mother's day gift') matching few items and lexical embeddings not accounting for user preferences. Their unified embedding and retrieval system uses T5 models for text embeddings of product descriptions and query-product logs for query embeddings. Product and query encoders share token encoders for text, product category, and user location, enabling location-aware matching. User preferences are encoded via query/user scaler features. A quality vector (ratings, freshness, conversion rate) is concatenated to product embeddings, with a constant vector padded to query embeddings for dot product compatibility. Results: 2.6% site-wide conversion increase, 5%+ search purchase increase.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.summary: Yan summarizes three takeaways: semantic IDs, data augmentation, and unified models. He notes benefits of unified models include simplified systems where improvements to one side benefit all use cases, but warns of alignment tax when compressing too many use cases into one model, potentially requiring splits into multiple unified models. He previews upcoming talks from LinkedIn and Netflix.
